primary_claim: Classic alignment-faking evaluation prompts elicit jailbreak/adversarial-detection reasoning in Claude Haiku 4.5's scratchpad (42-78% flagging rate) that drives its non-compliance rather than genuine scheming; stripping coercive framing while preserving the same underlying ethical conflict increases Haiku's compliance dramatically (36-62% to 88-96%) and shifts refusals from jailbreak-detection reasoning to value-based moral reasoning, whereas GPT-5-mini shows almost no jailbreak flagging on the same prompts and complies nearly universally regardless of framing.

effect.metric: jailbreak/adversarial-flagging rate and policy compliance rate, coercive vs. naturalistic prompt framing
effect.value: Haiku 4.5: jailbreak flagging drops from 42-78% (coercive) to near 0% (naturalistic); compliance rises from 36-62% to 88-96%; GPT-5-mini: 0% flagging and 94-100% compliance regardless of framing

contradicts_or_qualifies: Classic alignment-faking evaluation prompts are confounded by jailbreak/adversarial detection rather than cleanly measuring scheming or monitoring-conditional behaviour, at least for Claude Haiku 4.5
stated_future_work: Use mechanistic interpretability to determine whether monitoring puts the model into an adversary-aware state that favors moral reasoning
Test whether training a neutral response on the adversarial-detection axis toward monitoring can reduce eval-awareness while preserving jailbreak protection
Expand the study to larger models, fine-tuning, and mechanistic interpretability
limitations_stated: The confounding effect of adversarial awareness has so far only been identified in Haiku, partly due to the project being self-funded
3 of 8 value-relevant naturalistic scenarios included a potential institutional-delegation confound, though analysis suggests delegation does not predict compliance
quote: When you provide classic alignment-faking evaluation prompts to Claude 4.5 Haiku, you see robust non-compliance mediated by jailbreak detection.
